title: Load Balancing gRPC & HTTP/2 Across Kubernetes Pods
prompt: Your payment-ledger gRPC service runs on Kubernetes behind an AWS Network Load Balancer (L4). During a 10x traffic surge, HPA scales the backend from 4 to 24 pods, yet CPU stays at 98% on the original 4 pods while the 20 new pods sit at 3% CPU. Existing Java and Python gRPC clients keep sending 100% of their 45,000 RPS over their initial subchannels. Diagnose why L4 load balancing fails for HTTP/2 and design a zero-downtime fix.

spark.summary: gRPC multiplexes all 45,000 RPS over a single persistent HTTP/2 TCP subchannel per resolved IP, causing L4 AWS NLB to pin 100% of traffic on the original 4 pods after HPA scales to 24; switching to L7 Envoy/gRPC client-side round_robin with MAX_CONNECTION_AGE balances all 24 pods in <30s.
spark.keyTakeaway: Never rely on L4 load balancers for gRPC/HTTP2—use L7 per-RPC load balancing (Envoy or headless-service client round_robin) paired with jittered server MAX_CONNECTION_AGE + GOAWAY.
spark.byteSummary:
**Core Mechanics:** Unlike HTTP/1.1 (which opens many short-lived TCP connections), gRPC over **HTTP/2** multiplexes thousands of concurrent RPC streams over a **single long-lived TCP subchannel** per backend connection.

**Visual & Structural Flow:** Depicts HPA Scale 4 -> 24 Pods: L4 NLB Pinning vs. L7 Round-Robin + GOAWAY (gRPC Client (120x) -> Envoy L7 / Headless -> Orig 4 Pods -> New 20 Pods); gRPC Client (round_robin) / Envoy L7 -> 24 Pods w/ Jittered GOAWAY (120 gRPC Clients -> L7 Envoy / DNS -> 24 Backend Pods -> GOAWAY Grace).

**Trade-Offs & Production:** Using a standard Kubernetes `ClusterIP` (`kube-proxy` L4 iptables/IPVS) has the exact same TCP-pinning flaw as an AWS NLB—`kube-proxy` only picks a backend pod when the TCP socket is first established. Production gRPC platforms balance at **Layer 7 (per-RPC)** in one of two ways: **Option A — L7 Proxy / Service Mesh (Envoy / Linkerd / Istio)**: Route gRPC through Envoy L7.

**Failure Modes & Application:** L7 HTTP/2 balancing and `GOAWAY` connection aging are essential across modern RPC meshes: **High-QPS Microservice Meshes**: Preventing HPA scale-out starvation in Envoy, Istio, or Linkerd.

learningJourney.title: Why L4 load balancing fails for gRPC and HTTP/2
learningJourney.explanation: Unlike HTTP/1.1 (which opens many short-lived TCP connections), gRPC over **HTTP/2** multiplexes thousands of concurrent RPC streams over a **single long-lived TCP subchannel** per backend connection. An AWS Network Load Balancer (L4) only load-balances **new TCP connections**. When HPA scales backend pods from `4` to `24` during a `10×` surge (`45,000 RPS`), the `120` client pods keep all RPCs pinned on their existing 4 TCP sockets—leaving the 20 new pods at 3% CPU.
learningJourney.purpose: The mechanism: understand how Why L4 load balancing fails for gRPC and HTTP/2 works from first principles.

learningJourney.title: What happens when HTTP/2 subchannels pin to old pods
learningJourney.explanation:
L4 connection-level balancing under HTTP/2 causes severe skew:

1. **98% vs. 3% CPU Skew**: Original 4 pods saturate and drop requests while 20 newly scaled pods sit idle.
2. **TLS 1.3 Reconnect Storms**: Naively closing connections every few seconds without jitter triggers expensive TLS 1.3 mTLS handshake bursts.

learningJourney.title: Enterprise solution: L7 Envoy / Headless Client round_robin + MAX_CONNECTION_AGE
learningJourney.explanation:
Production gRPC platforms balance at **Layer 7 (per-RPC)** in one of two ways:

- **Option A — L7 Proxy / Service Mesh (Envoy / Linkerd / Istio)**: Route gRPC through Envoy L7 listeners that terminate HTTP/2 and multiplex per-RPC across all 24 dynamic `EndpointSlice` IPs.
- **Option B — Client-Side Lookaside / Headless DNS `round_robin`**: Expose a Kubernetes `clusterIP: None` headless service and configure Java (`grpc-netty`) and Python (`grpcio`) with `defaultServiceConfig: {"loadBalancingConfig": [{"round_robin": {}}]}` + periodic DNS refresh (`30 s`).
- **Jittered Server `MAX_CONNECTION_AGE`**: Configure gRPC servers with `maxConnectionAge = 5m` + `maxConnectionAgeGrace = 10s` + random jitter so servers emit HTTP/2 **`GOAWAY`** frames cleanly—draining 2s in-flight RPCs and forcing clients to rebalance onto new pods without TLS storms.

learningJourney.markdownContent:
```java
// Java grpc-netty: client-side round_robin + server MAX_CONNECTION_AGE
ManagedChannel channel = ManagedChannelBuilder
    .forTarget("dns:///payment-ledger-headless.prod.svc.cluster.local:9090")
    .defaultLoadBalancingPolicy("round_robin")
    .build();

Server server = NettyServerBuilder.forPort(9090)
    .maxConnectionAge(300 + ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextInt(60), TimeUnit.SECONDS)
    .maxConnectionAgeGrace(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS) // finishes 2s in-flight RPCs after GOAWAY
    .build();
```

learningJourney.title: Where gRPC L7 Load Balancing applies in System Design
learningJourney.explanation:
L7 HTTP/2 balancing and `GOAWAY` connection aging are essential across modern RPC meshes:

- **High-QPS Microservice Meshes**: Preventing HPA scale-out starvation in Envoy, Istio, or Linkerd.
- **ML Inference & Feature Stores**: Balancing heavy TensorFlow/Triton gRPC streams evenly across GPU replicas.
- **Headless Kubernetes Services**: Client-side `round_robin` / `xDS` proxyless gRPC without sidecar overhead.
